The rain had turned the bus into a steamy, packed box. Ishita, nine, held the rail with one hand and her little sister Tanuja’s wrist with the other. Mummy’s umbrella knocked a man’s elbow. “Sorry, that was my umbrella,” she said, and he nodded.
When the conductor held the bell so an old woman could climb down first, Mummy said, “Thank you, bhaiya.” Tanuja copied it in a loud little voice. A boy near the door pushed out without a word.
Later, Mummy waited her turn at the door, and as they got off, Ishita turned around. “Thank you,” she told the conductor. He looked surprised, then smiled.

qa.q: Why was Ishita holding Tanuja's wrist on the bus?
qa.a: The bus was packed, so Ishita kept hold of her little sister Tanuja's wrist while holding the rail with the other hand.

qa.q: What might Ishita have been thinking when she turned round to thank the conductor?
qa.a: Ishita probably felt a shy little pride and wanted to do what Mummy had done, since nobody told her to turn round and say thank you.

qa.q: What does Ishita's thank-you at the end suggest about what she learned on the bus?
qa.a: Nobody told Ishita to say it. She had watched Mummy apologise, wait and thank, and she did the same when she got the chance.

qa.q: How might the man whose elbow was bumped have felt about Mummy's apology?
qa.a: He may have felt his crowded discomfort ease a little, since a quick apology treated him as a person. He nodded, which suggests he accepted it.

grounding: Shows Mummy modelling thanks, patience and apology on a crowded bus, and a child copying without being told.

passage:
On Saturday, Elizabeth and her son Tanvir joined the long line at the vegetable weighing counter. Elizabeth waited without sighing while a man in front argued about a price. A woman’s bag swung and bumped Elizabeth’s arm. “Oh, sorry, I was in your way,” Elizabeth said, though it wasn’t her fault, and the woman laughed.
At the counter she said, “Thank you, that looks fresh,” and the young seller looked up and his tired face softened. Tanvir, eight, said nothing. He only watched.
On Monday at school, Tanvir bumped into a girl carrying books. “Sorry,” he said quickly, and bent to pick one up before anyone told him to.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth say to the seller at the counter?
qa.a: She said, “Thank you, that looks fresh.”

qa.q: What might the seller have been feeling when his face softened?
qa.a: The seller was probably feeling a little more appreciated after a long, tiring day. A simple thank-you from a customer in the line changed his mood.

qa.q: What choice did Tanvir make at school on Monday, and where might it have come from?
qa.a: He apologised at once and helped pick up the book without being told. He had seen Elizabeth do the same kind of thing at the market.

qa.q: How might the woman with the swinging bag have felt about Elizabeth's apology?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved that no one was angry, and even a little amused, since she laughed. Elizabeth's kindness turned a small bump into a friendly moment.

grounding: Shows Elizabeth's thanks, patient waiting and apology in a market line, and Tanvir later copying that manner at school.
